title: 01.1 Overview: registration is more than one step
text:
Starting a business in the Philippines usually involves several separate registrations:

1. **Business or entity registration** – DTI (sole proprietorship business name), SEC (corporations and partnerships), or CDA (cooperatives).
2. **Local permits and clearances** – the Mayor's Permit / business permit from the city or municipality, plus barangay and other clearances.
3. **BIR tax registration.**
4. **Sector-specific permits or licenses** – for example, FDA for food manufacturers.

title: 01.1 Overview: registration is more than one step
text:
**Key rule for the chatbot:** DTI business name registration does NOT by itself authorize a business to operate. It registers only the business name. The permit to operate is the business permit (Mayor's Permit) issued by the LGU.

(Status: VERIFIED, INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > What it is
text:
A sole proprietor registers a **business name** with DTI through the online **Business Name Registration System (BNRS)**: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/

- Business name registration has been fully online since August 1, 2023. DTI regional and provincial offices and Negosyo Centers can assist with online applications, renewals, and certification requests.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Who can register
text:
Any Filipino at least 18 years old can register a business name. Foreign nationals authorized to do business in the Philippines may also register.

(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Territorial scope and fees
text:
The fee depends on the territorial scope chosen:

| Territorial scope | Registration fee | Plus documentary stamp tax |
|---|---|---|
| Barangay | ₱200 | ₱30 |
| City/Municipality | ₱500 | ₱30 |
| Regional | ₱1,000 | ₱30 |
| National | ₱2,000 | ₱30 |

An additional 50% is charged for late filing (late renewal).

(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > How to choose the territorial scope (office guidance)
text: Territorial scope is based on where the business is **physically located** (its office, store, or branches), not where its customers are.

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > How to choose the territorial scope (office guidance)
text:
- One store in one barangay → Barangay scope. Example given: a sari-sari store in Barangay Irisan.
- Branches in more than one barangay within the same city (e.g., Irisan and Camp 8 in Baguio City) → City/Municipality scope. The fee is not multiplied per barangay.
- Branches using the same name in different cities/provinces within the region (e.g., Baguio and La Trinidad, Mountain Province, or Abra) → Regional scope.
- Nationwide → National scope.
- An online business with a single office but customers elsewhere (e.g., a client in Mindanao) may still register at Barangay scope, because scope follows the office location.

(Status: INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Validity and renewal
text:
- A DTI business name registration is valid for **5 years** from the date of registration.
- **Early renewal:** up to 180 calendar days before expiry.
- **Regular renewal:** within 90 calendar days after expiry.
- **Grace period:** within the next 90 calendar days after the regular period, with a 50% surcharge on the registration fee.
- A business name not renewed within the grace period is cancelled.
- The renewal fee follows the same territorial-scope schedule.
Source: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/faq (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Cancellation
text:
- Cancellation is done at selected DTI offices. Grounds listed by BNRS: the business stopped before expiry; the business was sold or transferred; someone else has prior rights to an identical or confusingly similar name; or the business moved outside its registered territorial scope.
- A DTI business name is **not transferable**. The registered owner's name must be cancelled before a new owner can register it. The office also mentioned cancellation after the owner's death.
Source: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/faq (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED, INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Amendments
text:
- Changing (upgrading) the territorial scope counts as a **new application**: a new certificate and a new 5-year validity.
- Changes of business address, owner's name, or civil status are made at a DTI office.
- Typos can be corrected only for a new registration, by emailing bnrshelpdesk@dtiphmail.dti.gov.ph.
- Transferring ownership is not allowed; cancel and register again under the new owner.
Source: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/faq (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Where to get help
text:
DTI provincial offices and Negosyo Centers (in municipalities) assist with business name registration. The DTI and Negosyo Center Facebook pages are also active channels.

(Status: INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > Names that are not allowed
text:
BNRS rejects names that, among other grounds: suggest unlawful or immoral activity; describe the quality of the goods or services; are already registered as a trade name, trademark, or business name; are purely generic words; are the names of other persons; or are deceptive or misleading.
- "Company", "Corporation", or "Incorporated" may be used only by SEC-registered partnerships or corporations.
- "Cooperative" may be used only by CDA-registered cooperatives.
Source: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/faq (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.2 DTI Business Name Registration (Sole Proprietorship) > How to pay and BNRS support
text:
- Payment: GCash, Maya, credit or debit card, over the counter (7-Eleven, Bayad Center), or Landbank Link.BizPortal. No other BNRS payment is needed after the registration fee.
- BNRS support: bnrs.support@dti.gov.ph; text or Viber 0917 595 3930.
Source: https://bnrs.dti.gov.ph/faq (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.3 SEC – Corporations and Partnerships
text:
The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) registers corporations (including One Person Corporations) and partnerships. Applications go through **eSPARC**: https://esparc.sec.gov.ph/application ; the **OneSEC** route is at https://esparc.sec.gov.ph/application/select-one-sec

Users should identify their intended business structure first, because the correct registration route depends on it.

(Status: FOR VALIDATION)
- DTI interview note: DTI also assists entrepreneurs with referrals for SEC registration. (INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.4 CDA – Cooperatives
text:
The Cooperative Development Authority (CDA) registers cooperatives through its online systems (e-CoopRIS): https://cs.cda.gov.ph/

Older CDA circulars (e.g., MC 2015-01) should not be treated as the only source of current requirements.

(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 01.4 CDA – Cooperatives > Name reservation and online registration
text:
- Before registering, a cooperative reserves its name with a Cooperative Name Reservation Notice: **₱100 for 30 days, ₱200 for 60 days, ₱300 for 90 days**.
- A cooperative becomes a legal entity when the CDA issues its Certificate of Registration.
- Register online through CDA's eCoopRIS: https://cs.cda.gov.ph/ecoopris/users/login
- The registration fee, minimum number of members, and training requirement are not on this page; ask the CDA.
Source: https://cda.gov.ph/services/regulatory-services/registration/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.5 Local Business Permits (overview only)
text: The business permit (Mayor's Permit) is the license to operate a business within a city or municipality. It is issued by the city or municipal government through its business permits and licensing office (in Baguio City, the Permits and Licensing Division, City Mayor's Office).

title: 01.5 Local Business Permits (overview only)
text:
What the office told us:
- After DTI registration, the entrepreneur proceeds to the city or municipal hall to get the Mayor's Permit.
- Typical supporting requirements include a **barangay clearance**, a **fire safety inspection certificate from the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP)**, a **sanitary permit**, and other requirements set by the LGU.
- Home-based and online businesses still need a business permit. A separate commercial office is not necessarily required, but there should be an identifiable place where the business is conducted. Specific requirements depend on the LGU.
- Fees and requirements differ between LGUs because each has its own revenue code (e.g., Baguio City vs. Tuba vs. La Trinidad), even for nearby places.

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration
text: Every business must register with the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR). Registering with DTI, SEC, CDA, or the LGU does not complete BIR registration.

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > When to register
text:
- Business taxpayers must register **on or before the start of business** (RA 11976, Ease of Paying Taxes Act; RR 7-2024; RMC No. 91-2024). Online sellers are included, with or without a physical store.
- Under RMC No. 91-2024, the start of business is counted from the **first sale**, or **30 calendar days after** the DTI business name certificate, SEC certificate, or Mayor's Permit is issued, **whichever comes first**. So do not wait for the Mayor's Permit before registering with BIR.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Which form
text:
- **BIR Form 1901**: sole proprietors, professionals, freelancers, online sellers, content creators, and other self-employed individuals.
- **BIR Form 1903**: corporations, partnerships, cooperatives, and associations.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Documentary requirements: sole proprietor (BIR checklist F1101, revised July 2025)
text:
Required:
1. BIR Form 1901, two originals (for manual applications).
2. One photocopy of a government-issued ID showing name, address, and birthdate. If the ID has no address, add proof of residence or business address. Online applicants upload a selfie holding the ID.
3. Invoices: either buy BIR Printed Invoices, or submit one final sample of your own invoices printed by an accredited printer.

If applicable:
- DTI business name certificate (photocopy).
- Special Power of Attorney and IDs if a representative files for you.
- BMBE Certificate of Authority, if registered as a Barangay Micro Business Enterprise.
- Work visa (foreign nationals); franchise documents (common carriers); proof of BOI/PEZA or similar registration.

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Documentary requirements: sole proprietor (BIR checklist F1101, revised July 2025)
text:
Fees: **₱30 documentary stamp tax** on the Certificate of Registration, plus the cost of BIR Printed Invoices if you buy them. The former ₱500 annual registration fee is no longer collected (see below).

- Incomplete applications are returned and not processed.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Where to register
text:
- **Online:** ORUS (Online Registration and Update System) at https://orus.bir.gov.ph/home. After paying the ₱30 DST online, you can generate an electronic Certificate of Registration (eCOR). Business registration in ORUS has been available since October 2024 (RMC 113-2024).
- **Other channels:** NewBizReg (https://web-services.bir.gov.ph/newbizreg/), the Philippine Business Hub (https://business.gov.ph/), or the New Business Registration counter of the Revenue District Office (RDO) covering your business address.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > After registration
text:
- **Display the Certificate of Registration** at the place of business. Businesses that sell through a website, social media, or another online platform must also display an electronic copy of their COR there. (RR 7-2024, as summarized by Grant Thornton) Status: FOR VALIDATION.
- **Books of accounts:** new businesses using manual books must register them before the deadline of the first quarterly or annual income tax return, whichever is earlier. (RMC 91-2024) Status: VERIFIED.
- **Invoices:** issue BIR-registered invoices for sales.

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Income tax options for sole proprietors
text:
- If gross sales and other non-operating income do **not exceed ₱3,000,000** a year and you are not VAT-registered, you may choose either:
  - **8% income tax** on gross sales/receipts **in excess of ₱250,000**. This replaces both the graduated income tax and the 3% percentage tax. No expense deductions. (The ₱250,000 reduction applies only to those earning purely from business, not mixed-income earners.)
  - **Graduated income tax rates** on net taxable income, **plus 3% percentage tax** on gross sales.
- The 8% option is chosen when registering (on Form 1901) or in the first quarterly return; otherwise the graduated rates apply automatically.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Taxpayer size classification (EOPT Act)
text:
- BIR classifies business taxpayers by gross sales: **micro** (below ₱3 million), **small** (₱3 million to below ₱20 million), **medium** (₱20 million to below ₱1 billion), **large** (₱1 billion and above). Micro and small taxpayers have lower penalties for some violations. (RR 8-2024; RR 6-2024, as summarized by KPMG and SunStar)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > The ₱500 Annual Registration Fee no longer applies
text:
Effective **January 22, 2024**, BIR stopped collecting the ₱500 Annual Registration Fee (ARF) under RA 11976. Business taxpayers no longer file BIR Form 0605 for the ARF, for new businesses or annual renewal.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.6 BIR Tax Registration > Closing a business with BIR
text:
- File BIR Form 1905 to close the business registration. Requirements include the form (two originals), a list of ending inventory, an inventory of unused invoices, and the original Certificate of Registration and other BIR permits. A ₱30 DST is affixed to the tax clearance issued for closure. (BIR checklist F1105C, July 2025)
- RMC No. 47-2026 streamlines closure procedures. A business that stops operating without closing its BIR registration stays liable for filing returns and paying taxes and penalties until closure is completed. (PwC Tax Alert No. 28, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED, FOR VALIDATION)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits (initial notes)
text:
- **Food businesses that manufacture, repack, import, distribute, or sell processed food under their own brand** need an FDA **License to Operate (LTO)**, and each processed food product needs a **Certificate of Product Registration (CPR)**. Details, fees, and steps are in 01.7 (FDA).
- Products should be properly labeled and packed. The DTI office raised this for trade fair participation (see 03.6).
- Other sector permits: PENDING research.
(Status: VERIFIED, INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA License to Operate (LTO): who needs it
text:
- An LTO is the FDA's permission for an establishment to manufacture, import, export, sell, or distribute food products.
- Food businesses that need one: **manufacturers**, **repackers**, toll manufacturers, distributors, importers, exporters, **traders** (own the brand but have a licensed manufacturer make it), and wholesalers. A distributor that sells to the general public is treated as a retailer.
- Applies to food businesses in Baguio City and Benguet like anywhere in the Philippines.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/faqs/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA License to Operate: how to apply
text:
- **Manufacturers** apply through the FDA e-Portal (https://eportal.fda.gov.ph). First request a user account by emailing fdac@fda.gov.ph, with a notarized authorization letter.
- **Distributors and traders** apply through FDA eServices (http://eservices.fda.gov.ph). No account needed; the email you declare cannot be changed later.
- Initial LTO requirements: the online application form (location plan, GPS coordinates, name of the Qualified Person); proof of business name registration (DTI certificate, SEC or CDA registration); the business permit if the address differs from the registration; and proof of capital (latest financial statement).
- If the application is disapproved, the payment is forfeited.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/faqs/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA License to Operate: fees
text:
LTO fees for **food manufacturers and traders**, by capital (initial for 2 years / renewal for 5 years):
| Capital | Initial | Renewal |
|---|---|---|
| ₱250,000 and below | ₱1,010 | ₱2,525 |
| Over ₱250,000, below ₱500,000 | ₱1,515 | ₱3,788 |
| ₱500,000, below ₱1 million | ₱2,020 | ₱5,050 |
| Over ₱1 million, below ₱5 million | ₱4,040 | ₱10,100 |
| ₱5 million, below ₱10 million | ₱6,060 | ₱15,150 |
Food distributors (importer, exporter, wholesaler): ₱8,080 initial, ₱20,200 renewal. Larger manufacturers pay more; see the FDA FAQ.
- Pay through Landbank, Bancnet, 7-Eleven, Bayad Center, or Landbank Link.BizPortal.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/faqs/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA License to Operate: validity, renewal, and penalties
text:
- An initial LTO is valid for **2 years**; a renewed LTO for **5 years** (bottled water renewals: 3 years).
- Renew within **90 days before** the expiry date.
- A renewal filed after expiry is charged a surcharge of **twice the renewal fee plus 10% per month**, up to 120 days. After 120 days the LTO is considered expired, and you must file a new initial application plus the penalties.
- To cancel an LTO or report that the business closed, send a letter to fdac.letters@fda.gov.ph.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/faqs/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA product registration (CPR)
text:
- Every processed food product (including food supplements, additives, and bottled water) that is manufactured, distributed, or repacked for sale needs an FDA **Certificate of Product Registration (CPR)** before it is sold.
- Apply through the FDA E-Registration system. Requirements include compliant labels, photos of the product from all angles, and the loose labels or artwork.
- The fee is computed by the system based on the product type and the validity applied for (2 to 5 years).
- Processing takes about **20 working days**.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/faqs/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.7 Sector-Specific Permits > FDA free LTO and product registration training for MSMEs (BBMSMEs)
text:
- The FDA's **Bigyang-halaga, Bangon MSMEs (BBMSMEs)** program helps micro, small, and medium food businesses and cosmetics makers get their LTO and product registration.
- It includes a **2-day training** by FDA experts on licensing, food product registration, and Good Manufacturing Practice, including how to use the FDA online systems.
- The FDA runs it with local governments: ask your city or municipal LGU in Baguio City or Benguet for the schedule, or email bbmsme@fda.gov.ph.
Source: https://www.fda.gov.ph/bbmsmes/ (program brochure) (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 01.8 General Registration Orientation (not a universal checklist)
text:
1. Identify your business structure (sole proprietorship, partnership, corporation, cooperative).
2. Register with the correct agency (DTI, SEC, or CDA).
3. Ask your city or municipality about business permit requirements (barangay clearance, fire safety, sanitary, and others).
4. Register with the BIR.
5. Get any additional licenses your business activity requires (e.g., FDA for food).
6. Keep your certificates, permits, receipts, and renewal dates on record.

title: 01.8 General Registration Orientation (not a universal checklist)
text:
**Office advice before registering:** Know your product AND your market. Identify your target customers and what makes your business different (unique selling point) before starting. (INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

This is an orientation only. Requirements and order may differ by LGU and business type.

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**Is DTI registration enough to start operating?**
No. DTI registration covers only your business name. You still need a business permit (Mayor's Permit) from your city or municipality, and BIR registration. *(VERIFIED / INTERVIEW-DERIVED)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**Should I register with DTI, SEC, or CDA?**
Sole proprietorship → DTI. Corporation or partnership → SEC. Cooperative → CDA. *(VERIFIED)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**Does DTI registration cover business taxes?**
No. Tax registration is done separately with the BIR. *(VERIFIED)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**Do I still pay the ₱500 annual BIR registration fee?**
No. BIR stopped collecting it effective January 22, 2024 (RMC No. 14-2024). *(VERIFIED)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**How much does DTI registration cost?**
₱200 (barangay), ₱500 (city/municipality), ₱1,000 (regional), or ₱2,000 (national), plus ₱30 documentary stamp tax. Check the BNRS for current rates. *(VERIFIED as of Nov 16, 2026)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**I sell online and have customers all over the country. Do I need national scope?**
Not necessarily. According to DTI Baguio–Benguet, scope follows where your office or branches are located, not where your customers are. One office in one barangay can use barangay scope. *(INTERVIEW-DERIVED)*

**How long is DTI registration valid?**
5 years. Late renewal has a 50% surcharge. *(VERIFIED)*

title: 01.9 Common Questions – Business Registration
text:
**Can I transfer my business name to someone else?**
No. The name must be cancelled first before someone else can register it. *(INTERVIEW-DERIVED)*

**Where do I register a corporation?** SEC, through eSPARC. *(FOR VALIDATION)*

**Where do I register a cooperative?** CDA. *(FOR VALIDATION)*

title: 02.1 What the business permit is
text:
- The business permit (Mayor's Permit) is the license to operate a business in Baguio City. DTI business name registration alone does not allow a business to operate. (See 01.1.)
- Baguio's PLD has stated that a business without a permit should not operate, based on the city tax ordinance. In 2023 the city issued 2,575 closure orders for non-compliance, and from January 1 to May 15, 2024 it shut down 544 businesses operating without permits. (Manila Bulletin, May 2024)
- **Online and home-based sellers also need a permit.** In 2020 the PLD head said all online businesses must secure a business permit, whether or not the owner is a student. (Baguio City Guide, May 28, 2020)
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.2 Where to apply
text:
- **Online:** the city's Electronic Business Permits and Licensing System (eBPLS) at https://ebpls.baguio.gov.ph. Baguio began accepting new applications online on July 18, 2022. Applicants register with an active email address, then log in to fill out the form and upload documents. After payment is verified, the permit is sent by email for printing. (Northern Philippine Times / PNA, August 2022)
- **In person:** Permits and Licensing Division, 1st Floor, Left Wing, Baguio City Hall. Satellite Business One-Stop Shops (BOSS) have operated in major malls (for example Baguio Centermall) for renewals.
- **Assessment app:** "Baguio in My Pocket" (BIMP) has been used for online tax assessments.
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.3 Documentary requirements for a new business permit
text: - **New requirement (2026):** the CHSO announced that businesses must have pest control measures in place to obtain or renew a permit. This means a vermin abatement program and a contract with a pest control operator licensed by the Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority; do-it-yourself pest control does not count. (Manila Bulletin, May 27, 2026). Effective date not stated; confirm with CHSO.

title: 02.3 Documentary requirements for a new business permit
text:
- **Small businesses with building or zoning problems:** under a 2009 administrative order, the city may still issue a permit in special cases, including sari-sari stores or small-scale businesses, or where the applicant has proof of right of possession. Since 2021, new businesses with deficiencies can get permits if they fix them within one year. A business permit is not a substitute for a building permit. (PNA)
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.4 Process for a new permit ("3Ps": Present, Pay, Print)
text:
1. **Present:** submit the complete documents to the PLD (or upload them on eBPLS). Presenting documents takes about 10 minutes when complete.
2. **Pay:** pay the assessed fees and taxes at the City Treasurer's Office (or online through eBPLS).
3. **Print:** return to the PLD to print the permit (online applicants receive it by email).

- The PLD has said processing takes about 20 minutes for new applications and 10 minutes for renewals when requirements are complete. (Manila Bulletin, May 2024)
- Under RA 11032 (Ease of Doing Business Act), LGUs must act on business permit applications within the prescribed processing times. (See feasibility context 1.3.)
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.5 Renewal
text:
- A business permit is valid for one year and must be renewed every year. (RA 11032; Local Government Code)
- **Baguio 2026 renewal schedule (by the owner's family or corporate name):** January 2–31 for A to H; February 1–28 for I to P; March 1–20 for Q to Z and names starting with numbers or special characters. Renewals outside the assigned month were not accepted. (City Treasurer's advisory, reported December 2025)
- **From January 2, 2026, renewal assessments are available only online through eBPLS.** City Hall no longer issues printed assessments. If eBPLS shows "No Record Found," bring a screenshot and supporting documents (income tax returns, financial statements, proof of gross receipts) to the Treasury Office.

title: 02.5 Renewal
text:
- **Payment options (2026):** online through eBPLS; bank deposit or transfer to the City Government of Baguio's Land Bank account, with proof emailed to the Treasury Office; or a manager's/cashier's check payable to the City Treasurer. Receipts or permits from bank payments can be claimed after at least five working days.
- **Late renewal:** penalties apply when renewal is not done within the assigned period. The official eBPLS portal states that late business tax payments incur a surcharge of up to 25% plus 2% interest per month (see 02.1A).
- **The schedule changes every year.** The chatbot must not present the 2026 schedule as permanent; it should tell users to check the current year's City Treasurer advisory.
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.6 Other permit transactions
text:
- Changes of location, management, or trade name, adding a line of business, partial retirement, and business retirement (closure) are handled at City Hall. (Baguio Midland Courier, 2024)
- Closing a business also requires closing the BIR registration; see 01.6.
(Status: FOR VALIDATION)

title: 02.7 Other Benguet LGUs
text:
- Each municipality (for example La Trinidad, Itogon, Tuba) has its own revenue code, fees, and procedures. (DTI interview)
- Example: Itogon's revenue code sets the renewal deadline without penalty at January 20; for 2026 the LGU extended it to January 30. (LGU Itogon, January 22, 2026)
- The chatbot should direct users outside Baguio City to their municipal BPLO or Negosyo Center.
(Status: VERIFIED, PENDING)

text:
**I only sell online from home. Do I still need a business permit in Baguio?**
Yes. Baguio's PLD has stated that online businesses must secure a business permit, including student sellers. (FOR VALIDATION)

text:

No. DTI registers your business name. You still need a business permit from the city and BIR registration. (VERIFIED)

Settlement can take up to 24 hours and a confirmation is emailed; do not pay twice while waiting. (VERIFIED, official eBPLS portal, Nov 17, 2026)

title: 03.1 DTI's three main functions
text:
According to the office, DTI's work is grouped into:
- **Trabaho** – helping businesses improve operations so they can provide jobs and livelihood in communities.
- **Negosyo** – business registration, training, market access, financing referrals, investments, and business counseling.
- **Konsyumer** – consumer protection (see Section 09 for complaints and referrals).

The office also has an **Industry** division that supports priority industries.

text:
Negosyo Centers are DTI's satellite offices located in municipalities. They provide registration help, counseling, and access to DTI programs.

- DTI's target is to have a Negosyo Center in every municipality by 2028. In Baguio and Benguet, the remaining municipalities without one were Bakun and Bokod (as of Nov 2026).

Negosyo Centers are set up under the Go Negosyo Act (RA 10644) to promote ease of doing business and help MSMEs access services. They are located in DTI offices, LGUs, schools, NGOs, and malls.

title: 03.5 DTI programs > Shared Service Facilities (SSF)
text:
- DTI provides machines, equipment, tools, and systems that are housed by a **cooperator** and shared with MSMEs to raise productivity and quality.
- Cooperators can be government entities (LGUs, state universities, tech-voc schools), private entities (cooperatives, associations, NGOs, people's organizations, corporations, private schools), or One Person Corporations. Individual MSMEs use the facility; they do not own it.
- Implemented by DTI regional and provincial offices. National contact: SSF Project Management Office, DTI-BSMED, BSMED@dti.gov.ph, (02) 7791-3310.
Source: https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-business-center/dti-programs-projects/dti-shared-service-facilities/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs > OTOP Next Gen
text:
OTOP Next Gen helps MSMEs that already have a "minimum viable product" improve quality, design, packaging, standards compliance, and marketability. Contact otop@dti.gov.ph or the local DTI office.
Source: https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-business-center/dti-programs-projects/dti-otop-philippines (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs > Kapatid Mentor ME: who can join
text:
- A 10-module mentoring program of DTI and the Philippine Center for Entrepreneurship, where large companies mentor micro and small entrepreneurs.
- Applicants: at least 18; Filipino resident; owner, co-owner, or partner of a registered business operating at least 1 year; has employees or manages a team; willing to attend all sessions and sign a Contract of Commitment; three references. One mentee per enterprise and per family.
- Online sessions need a computer or phone, stable internet, a headset, and a Facebook account.
- Apply through the nearest Negosyo Center or DTI office.
Source: https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-business-center/dti-programs-projects/dti-kapatid-mentor-me-project/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs > Youth Entrepreneurship Program (YEP)
text:
- Based on the Youth Entrepreneurship Act (RA 10679). For aspiring and existing youth entrepreneurs aged 18–30.
- **Youth Start:** mindset seminars, help with business registration, skills training.
- **Youth Net:** mentoring and youth entrepreneur organizations.
- **Youth Match:** market promotion, access to funding, machines and equipment.
- Apply through a DTI office or Negosyo Center.
Source: https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-business-center/dti-programs-projects/dti-youth-entrepreneurship-program-yep/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.1 Negosyo Centers (RA 10644, Go Negosyo Act)
text:
Negosyo Centers provide four groups of services:
- **Business registration help:** processing new and renewal registrations, including Barangay Micro Business Enterprise (BMBE) registration, and coordinating with LGUs and agencies.
- **Business advisory:** help meeting regulatory requirements, market links, access to grants and shared equipment, and mentoring programs.
- **Information and advocacy:** information on training, financing, and marketing; support for youth and women entrepreneurs.
- **Monitoring and evaluation:** feedback channels and process improvements for MSMEs.

(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.2 Kapatid Mentor ME (KMME)
text:
- A joint program of DTI and the Philippine Center for Entrepreneurship (Go Negosyo), running since 2016.
- A **10-module mentorship program** with weekly sessions where business owners and practitioners mentor micro and small entrepreneurs on areas such as marketing, finance, operations, and business planning. Some regions run it online (KMME–Money Market Encounter).
- Goals: help micro and small entrepreneurs scale up, create jobs, and prepare OTOP entrepreneurs for expansion.
- Who can join: regional calls typically require the business to have been **operating for at least one year** with complete business registration. It is **free**.
- How to join: watch for calls for mentees from the DTI provincial office or Negosyo Center.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.2 Kapatid Mentor ME (KMME)
text: - Note: in the DTI interview, a "10-module" program was mentioned next to the Youth Entrepreneurship Program. Official sources describe KMME as the 10-module program; YEP's standard workshop has 4 modules (see 03.5.5).

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.3 OTOP Next Gen (One Town, One Product Next Generation)
text:
- OTOP has two parts: **OTOP Next Gen** (supply side) gives MSMEs a package of help to improve their products, and **OTOP Philippines Hub / OTOP.PH** (demand side) gives physical and online stores to sell them.
- OTOP Next Gen covers product development, design, packaging and labeling, branding, training, and market matching, to improve design, quality, and volume.
- It is for MSMEs that already have a **minimum viable product** and are ready to level up; businesses just starting out are helped through other DTI programs.
- Selection usually starts with an assessment and screening session (sometimes called an ACT session: Assessment, Consultation and Triage).

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.3 OTOP Next Gen (One Town, One Product Next Generation)
text:
- The Cordillera received about ₱6.26 million for OTOP Next Gen in one year's budget (PNA).
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.4 Shared Service Facilities (SSF)
text:
- DTI provides machines, equipment, and tools that MSMEs share, to raise productivity.
- **Cooperators** run the facility. They can be government (LGUs, agencies, state universities, technical schools) or private (NGOs, people's organizations, cooperatives, industry associations).
- Cooperator requirements: willing to open the facility to MSMEs; provide a building, staff, and working capital; private groups must be registered with SEC, CDA, or similar and have at least **two years** of track record.
- **Individuals cannot apply** to receive an SSF and cannot take machines home. Individual MSMEs use the facility by schedule and **pay a usage fee** set by the cooperator.

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.4 Shared Service Facilities (SSF)
text:
- DTI keeps ownership and grants the cooperator the right to use the equipment for two years (usufruct). Ownership may be donated to the cooperator if the project succeeds.
- How to apply: send a proposal to the nearest DTI regional or provincial office. Projects up to ₱5 million are approved regionally.
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.5 DTI programs: overview > 03.5.5 Youth Entrepreneurship Program (YEP)
text:
- Legal basis: **RA 10679, Youth Entrepreneurship Act**.
- For aspiring and existing Filipino entrepreneurs aged **18 to 30**.
- Three parts: **Youth Start** (mindset, business registration help, seminars, skills training), **Youth Net** (mentoring, networks, youth business groups), **Youth Match** (access to markets, funding, equipment).
- The standard workshop, **"YEP! You Can Be Your Own Boss" (YEP-BYOB)**, covers 4 modules (My Business, Business Operations, My Resources and Finances, My Business Pitch) with 19 topics, often ending with a pitch competition.
- How to join: ask the DTI provincial office or a Negosyo Center; DTI's Bureau of SME Development can be reached at BSMED@dti.gov.ph.

- In the Cordillera, DTI and CHED ran a YEP-based project ("Project MARITES") for young entrepreneurs (PIA CAR, 2024).
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 03.6 Joining a trade fair
text:
- **Food products:** Manufacturers need FDA registration and a License to Operate (LTO), valid permits, and properly labeled and packed products.
- **Non-food products:** Requirements depend on the product.
- **Costs:** Participants pay the trade fair participation fee. Travel, accommodation (e.g., for Manila fairs), and meals are shouldered by the participant and are not covered by DTI.

(Status: INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 03.7 Office advice to new entrepreneurs
text:
- Know both your product and your market before starting. A good product without a target market will not grow.
- Find your unique selling point. Example given: many sari-sari stores sell the same items, so think about what would make yours different, such as wifi, air conditioning, or a place for customers to hang out.

(Status: INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 04.1 DTI does not give capital
text:
DTI does not give cash or start-up capital to businesses. It helps entrepreneurs start or improve their businesses through training, referrals, and assistance.

(Status: INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

- If an MSME wants a loan, it can approach DTI or a Negosyo Center. DTI refers it to a financing partner that fits the business's needs. (INTERVIEW-DERIVED)

title: 04.2 Loans through SB Corporation and partner institutions > Pondo sa Pagbabago at Pag-asenso (P3)
text:
- P3 is a government microfinancing program run through SB Corp, meant to give microenterprises an alternative to informal "5-6" lending.
- P3 loans are given through **partner financial institutions** (such as microfinance institutions and cooperatives), not directly by SB Corp. Apply through a partner institution.
- Loans to microenterprises, including farming activities, are **₱5,000 to ₱300,000**, with interest and fees up to **2.5% a month (30% a year)**.

title: 04.2 Loans through SB Corporation and partner institutions > Barangay Micro Business Enterprise (BMBE)

- Under RA 10644, Negosyo Centers handle BMBE registration. (See 03.)

text:
- SB Corp RISE UP and P3 are **loans** that must be repaid.
- DTI does **not** give grants or cash capital. Disaster assistance through PPG is given **in kind** (equipment or stocks), not cash. (See 04.1 and 04.3.)

title: 04.5 Agricultural loans > KAYA loans for young agripreneurs
text:

- For agri-fishery entrepreneurs aged **18 to 30** who are graduates of agriculture or fishery courses or programs (formal or non-formal).
- Requirements: government ID, loan application form, simple business plan, proof of RSBSA or FFEDIS registration.
- Apply at https://access.acpc.gov.ph. Applications go to a partner lender (cooperative, cooperative bank, or rural bank).

title: 04.5 Agricultural loans > SURE loans after calamities
text:
- DA-ACPC's Survival and Recovery loan: up to **₱25,000**, 0% interest (up to 3% service fee), no collateral, payable up to 3 years.
- For small farmers and fisherfolk in areas under a **state of calamity**, enrolled in RSBSA.
- Borrowers are identified and endorsed by the DA regional office and the Municipal Agriculture Office; there is no direct application.

title: 05.1 Livelihood assistance versus business loans
text:
- Livelihood programs from DSWD and DOLE are **grants** (mostly in kind or as seed capital) for poor, vulnerable, or low-income people. They are not loans.
- They are different from DTI's business services (Section 03) and from SB Corp loans (Section 04). The chatbot should first find out whether the user is looking for a loan, a grant, or training.

title: 05.2 DSWD Sustainable Livelihood Program (SLP)
text:
- **What it is:** a capability-building program of DSWD for poor, vulnerable, and marginalized households. It has two tracks:
  - **Microenterprise Development (MD) track:** helps start or grow a microenterprise through seed capital, skills training, and building livelihood assets.
  - **Employment Facilitation (EF) track:** helps participants who are ready for jobs find employment.
- **Seed Capital Fund (SCF):** start-up capital for small tools, raw materials, and shared equipment needed to start or expand a microenterprise. It has been reported at up to **₱15,000 per family** (DSWD presentation; Philstar 2020).

title: 05.2 DSWD Sustainable Livelihood Program (SLP)
text:
- **Who can join:** members of poor, marginalized, vulnerable, or disadvantaged households identified by DSWD (for example through its household targeting system or as 4Ps families). Individual referrals and walk-in clients are handled under special guidelines (DSWD MC 14, s. 2018).
- **How to apply:** through the city or municipal social welfare office or the DSWD field office. Under the MD track, participants submit a proposal that is assessed before funds are released.
- Since 2011, SLP has assisted over 3.3 million beneficiaries (PNA, February 2024).
- **In Baguio:** start with the City Social Welfare and Development Office (CSWDO). Contact details: PENDING.
(Status: VERIFIED, FOR VALIDATION)

title: 05.3 DOLE Integrated Livelihood Program (DILP / Kabuhayan Program)
text:
- **What it is:** a DOLE program that gives grant assistance for livelihood and entrepreneurship to vulnerable and marginalized workers, for individuals or groups. It is part of DOLE's Integrated Livelihood and Emergency Employment Program (DILEEP), together with TUPAD (emergency employment).
- **Components:**
  - **Kabuhayan Formation:** start a new individual or group livelihood.
  - **Kabuhayan Enhancement:** grow an existing livelihood into a sustainable business.
  - **Kabuhayan Restoration:** rebuild livelihoods damaged by calamities.

title: 05.3 DOLE Integrated Livelihood Program (DILP / Kabuhayan Program)
text:
- **Who can join (examples):** self-employed workers with insufficient income; unpaid family workers; low-wage, seasonal, or displaced workers; marginalized farmers and fisherfolk; women, youth, persons with disabilities, senior citizens, and Indigenous Peoples; parents of child laborers; rebel returnees. DO 239-B (2026) added more groups, including TESDA graduates and micro-entrepreneurs who completed DOLE technical advisory visits.
- **Not eligible:** 4Ps beneficiaries and government employees (per DOLE regional guidance).
- **Assistance (DOLE regional guidance):**

| Group, micro (15–25 members) | up to ₱250,000 |

title: 05.3 DOLE Integrated Livelihood Program (DILP / Kabuhayan Program)

Group projects need a management team and a profit-sharing scheme in the business plan.
- **How to apply:** through DOLE-accredited co-partners (ACPs), such as LGUs (often through the PESO), cooperatives, or organizations, which submit the proposal or business plan to DOLE. DTI can help prepare the proposal (INTERVIEW-DERIVED, see 04.4).

title: 07. Marketing and Business Management
text: Note for the chatbot: this section is general advice. When answering from it, say it is general guidance and suggest a Negosyo Center for business counseling.

title: 07.1 Before starting: know your product and your market
text:
- Know both your product and your market. Identify your target customers and what makes your business different (unique selling point). A good product without a target market will not grow. (DTI Baguio–Benguet interview)
- Example from DTI: many sari-sari stores sell the same goods, so think about what would make yours stand out.

title: 07.2 The business plan
text:
- DTI's guide for new entrepreneurs (developed with the UP Institute for Small-Scale Industries and the BSP) organizes a business plan into four parts: **marketing plan** (customers, competitors, pricing, promotion), **technical plan** (production, suppliers, equipment, location), **organizational plan** (people, roles, registration), and **financial plan** (start-up costs, projected income, cash flow).
- DTI's online MSME Resources section has guides on writing a business plan, registration requirements, food hygiene and packaging, bookkeeping, and financing. Business counselors at Negosyo Centers can help.
(Status: VERIFIED, GENERAL GUIDANCE)

title: 07.3 Pricing, records, and money
text:
- Learn basic **costing and pricing** so prices cover costs and leave a profit; DTI offices hold free costing and pricing workshops.
- Keep **records** of sales and expenses. Registered businesses must keep BIR-registered books of accounts (see 01.6) and issue invoices.
- Keep business money separate from household money.
(Status: GENERAL GUIDANCE)

title: 07.4 Rules for selling: prices and labels
text:
- Follow consumer rules enforced by DTI, such as the Price Tag Act, proper product labeling, and the ban on giving candy instead of coins as change. Sales promotions need a DTI permit. (DTI interview; see 09.3)
- Packaged food must meet FDA requirements; see 01.7.

title: 07.4 Rules for selling > Sales promotion permits from DTI
text:
- Sales promos (raffles, contests, discounts with conditions) need a **DTI sales promotion permit**.
- Nationwide and NCR promos are applied for online through DTI's **IRegIS** (https://iregis.dti.gov.ph; sign up as a Negosyo Applicant). You first need a **NegosyoKonek Reference Number** (https://negosyokonek.dti.gov.ph, "Konek Your Business"), created once per business; sole proprietors, partnerships, corporations, and cooperatives can all get one.
- IRegIS covers only nationwide and NCR promos. For a promo only in Baguio City or Benguet, ask DTI Benguet or the nearest Negosyo Center.
- Contact: DTI Fair Trade Enforcement Bureau, Sales Promotion Division, (02) 8811-8233, FTEB@dti.gov.ph.
Source: https://www.dti.gov.ph/dti-consumer-space/dti-newly-accredited-licensed-business/dti-sales-promotion-application (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 07.5 Selling online: the Internet Transactions Act (RA 11967)
text:
- RA 11967, the **Internet Transactions Act of 2023**, protects online consumers and merchants. DTI regulates e-commerce through its new **E-Commerce Bureau**.
- The law took full effect on **June 20, 2025**, when its 18-month transition period ended. DTI can now issue compliance orders, take down websites, and blacklist or fine non-compliant online sellers.
- Online merchants are primarily liable to consumers for complaints about their online sales; the platform is liable only in a secondary way.
- The E-Commerce Bureau keeps an **Online Business Database** of online merchants and platforms.
- Online sellers in Baguio also need a city business permit (02.1) and BIR registration, and must display their BIR certificate online (01.6).

title: 07.5 Selling online: the Internet Transactions Act (RA 11967)
text:
- Consumer-to-consumer selling is outside the law's stated coverage.
(Status: VERIFIED, FOR VALIDATION)

- Use digital channels; DTI and DICT offer digitalization trainings.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**I want to start a small business in Baguio. What are the steps?**
In general: (1) choose your business structure; (2) register the name with DTI (sole proprietor) or register with SEC or CDA; (3) get your barangay clearance and other clearances, then apply for the Mayor's Permit at the Baguio PLD or online through eBPLS; (4) register with BIR on or before you start selling; (5) get any special licenses, such as FDA for food. See 01.8, 02, and 01.6. Ask a Negosyo Center for help with your specific case.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**Do I register with BIR before or after getting my Mayor's Permit?**
Don't wait for the Mayor's Permit. BIR registration is due on or before the start of business, counted from your first sale or 30 days after your DTI, SEC, or Mayor's Permit document is issued, whichever comes first. See 01.6.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**I only sell online. What do I need?**
A DTI business name (if you use a business name), a Baguio business permit (online sellers are covered), and BIR registration, with your BIR certificate displayed on your online page. The Internet Transactions Act also covers online merchants. See 01.2, 02.1, 01.6, and 07.5.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**Should I choose the 8% income tax?**
If your yearly gross sales are ₱3 million or less and you are not VAT-registered, you can choose 8% on sales above ₱250,000 (for purely self-employed individuals) or graduated rates plus 3% percentage tax. Which is better depends on your expenses. See 01.6 and ask the BIR or an accountant.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**Can I get a government loan for my business?**
SB Corp (DTI's financing arm) offers loans for MSMEs, applied for online; P3 has offered small collateral-free microloans. Terms change, so check SB Corp or a Negosyo Center. See 04.2.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**I am poor and want to start a small livelihood. Is there free assistance?**
DSWD's Sustainable Livelihood Program and DOLE's Kabuhayan (DILP) give livelihood grants, often as starter kits or seed capital, to qualified low-income or vulnerable people. Ask the City Social Welfare and Development Office or DOLE. See 05.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**My store burned down. Can DTI help?**
DTI's PPG program can give in-kind help (stocks or equipment) to microenterprises hit by fire or disasters, depending on budget. See 04.3.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**Where can I learn a skill for free?**
TESDA scholarships (TWSP, STEP) offer free training and assessment; STEP includes starter toolkits. In Baguio, contact TESDA CSITE (Loakan Road) or the TESDA Baguio–Benguet office. See 06.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**Can my group get equipment from DTI?**
Through DTI's Shared Service Facilities, a registered organization (such as a cooperative or association with at least 2 years of track record) can run DTI-provided equipment for MSMEs to use. Individuals can only use an SSF, not receive one. See 03.5.4.

title: 08.2 Common questions across topics
text:
**How do I report a store that overcharges or sells defective goods?**
Report to DTI. You may report anonymously if your claim is factual and has evidence. See 09.3.

Not covered. DTI business name fees (01.2) apply only to sole proprietorships and are not SEC fees. Ask the SEC or check the fee computed in eSPARC: https://esparc.sec.gov.ph/application. (See 01.3.)

Not covered. The amount is assessed by the City Treasurer's Office under the Baguio revenue code, based on the line of business and gross sales. Get the assessment through eBPLS (https://ebpls.baguio.gov.ph) or ask the City Treasurer's Office. BIR income tax (8% or graduated rates, see 01.6) is a different, national tax.

title: 10.1 Hiring employees > Overview
text:
- When a business hires its first employee, it must register as an employer with **SSS**, **PhilHealth**, and **Pag-IBIG**, and follow DOLE wage rules.
- The **Central Business Portal (https://business.gov.ph)** has one employee-reporting module covering SSS, PhilHealth, and Pag-IBIG.
- A self-employed owner who hires workers must also register as an employer and get an SSS Employer Number.
Source: https://www.sss.gov.ph/employer-er/ and https://www.sss.gov.ph/self-employed/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 10.2 Hiring employees > SSS employer registration
text:
- SSS coverage of an employer starts on the **first day of operation**.
- Register through the Central Business Portal (no SS Form R-1 or supporting documents needed), through My.SSS online, or at an SSS branch.
- Report new employees to SSS **within 30 days from their hiring date**. Employees must have their own SS numbers.
- Each month, deduct the employee share from pay and remit it with the employer share and EC contribution, using a Payment Reference Number (PRN).
- Late contributions are charged a **2% penalty per month** until paid.
- Contribution rates are in the SSS contribution table (effective January 1, 2025): https://www.sss.gov.ph/sss-contribution-table/
Source: https://www.sss.gov.ph/employer-er/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 10.3 Hiring employees > SSS for self-employed owners
text:
- A self-employed SSS member is someone who has no employer other than themself.
- Contributions are paid monthly or quarterly using a PRN from My.SSS. The deadline is the **last day of the month after** the month being paid for.
- Amounts follow the latest SSS schedule of contributions.
Source: https://www.sss.gov.ph/self-employed/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 10.4 Hiring employees > PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG
text:
- Private-sector workers with an employer–employee relationship are covered under PhilHealth's formal economy program. The member submits a PhilHealth Member Registration Form.
- Employer registration steps and premium rates for PhilHealth, and employer registration and contribution rates for Pag-IBIG, are not covered here. Ask PhilHealth or Pag-IBIG, or register through the Central Business Portal (https://business.gov.ph).
Source: https://www.philhealth.gov.ph/members/formal/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 10.5 Hiring employees > Minimum wage in Baguio City and Benguet (Cordillera, CAR)
text:
- Baguio City and all Benguet towns (including La Trinidad, Tuba, and Itogon) are in the Cordillera Administrative Region (CAR), so the CAR wage orders apply.
- Private sector: **₱505.00 per day** under **Wage Order No. CAR-24**, effective **December 30, 2025**.
- Domestic workers (kasambahay): **₱6,600.00 per month** under **Wage Order No. CAR-DW-07**, effective December 30, 2025.
- Wage orders change. Check the National Wages and Productivity Commission for the current order: https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/
Source: https://nwpc.dole.gov.ph/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 11.1 Customer discounts > PWD discount: what businesses must give
text:
- Persons with disabilities get **at least 20% discount and VAT exemption** (if applicable) on goods and services for their exclusive use, including: hotels, restaurants, and recreation centers; admission to theaters, cinemas, and similar venues; medicines in drugstores; medical and dental services; domestic air and sea fares; land transport fares; and funeral and burial services. (RA 10754)
- Proof: a PWD ID issued by the city or municipal mayor or barangay captain, the PWD's passport, or a transportation discount ID from the national council.
- The PWD discount cannot be combined with a higher discount or another discount program.
Source: https://ncda.gov.ph/disability-laws/republic-acts/republic-act-no-10754-an-act-expanding-the-benefits-and-privileges-of-persons-with-disability-pwd/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 11.1 Customer discounts > PWD discount: tax deduction for the business
text:
- A business can claim the PWD discount it gave (except on government medical services) as a **tax deduction**, based on the net cost of the goods sold or services rendered, in the same taxable year, with proper documentation. (RA 10754)
- For the senior citizen discount, see 11.2.
Source: https://ncda.gov.ph/disability-laws/republic-acts/republic-act-no-10754-an-act-expanding-the-benefits-and-privileges-of-persons-with-disability-pwd/ (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 11.2 Customer discounts > Senior citizen discount: what businesses must give
text:
- Senior citizens (resident Filipino citizens aged **60 or older**) get a **20% discount and VAT exemption** (if applicable) on goods and services for their exclusive use, including: medicines and some vaccines; doctors' fees and medical, dental, and lab services in private facilities; land transport, domestic air and sea fares; **hotels and lodging, restaurants, and recreation centers**; admission to theaters, cinemas, and amusement places; and funeral and burial services. (RA 9994)
- Applies to businesses in Baguio City and Benguet like everywhere in the Philippines.
Source: https://www.ncsc.gov.ph/post/what-are-the-rights-and-privileges-of-senior-citizens (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 11.2 Customer discounts > Senior citizen discount: proof, promos, and combining discounts
text:
- Proof the senior can show: an **OSCA ID** (from the Office of Senior Citizens Affairs; honored nationwide), a passport, or other documents proving citizenship and age 60+.
- If an item is already on promo, the senior gets either the promo discount or the 20% discount, **whichever is higher**, not both.
- The National Commission of Senior Citizens says discounts follow the rules on promotional discounts and the prohibition on combining discounts, after an October 2026 Supreme Court ruling.
- NCSC contact: (02) 8567-5646, contact@ncsc.gov.ph.
Source: https://www.ncsc.gov.ph/post/what-are-the-rights-and-privileges-of-senior-citizens and https://www.ncsc.gov.ph/post/pahayag-ng-ncsc-sa-no-double-discount-ruling-ng-korte-suprema (checked November 23, 2026)
(Status: VERIFIED)

title: 11.2 Customer discounts > Senior citizen discount: tax deduction for the business
text:
- A business can claim the senior citizen discounts it gave as a **tax deduction**, based on the cost of the goods sold or services rendered, in the same taxable year. The amount, net of VAT, must be included in gross sales receipts and properly documented under the Tax Code. (RA 9994)
Source: https://www.ncsc.gov.ph/post/what-are-the-rights-and-privileges-of-senior-citizens (checked November 23, 2026)
